summary: A wooden tower on an iron caisson at the mouth of Cold Spring Harbor, lit in 1890; moved ashore to private land in 1965, with the caisson left at the site.

light.characteristic: fixed white with fixed red sector (from 31 May 1892)

structures.type: square pyramidal wooden tower on caisson
structures.status: moved ashore to private land on Centre Island in 1965
structures.note: 38 ft from base to center of lantern (USLHS)

structures.type: steel skeleton tower on the caisson

access.note: Privately owned; grounds and tower closed. Centre Island is a gated community. The caisson can be seen from Lloyd Beach.

facts.agency: United States Coast Guard (maintenance from 1948, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Congress appropriates $20,000 and approves two range lights on the mainland (LighthouseFriends; not in the corpus).
Light House Service opts for a lighthouse on the shoal instead of range lights (Bachand).
Construction begins in late summer 1889 with the caisson.
Wooden tower finished on the caisson.
Fixed red changed to fixed white with a fixed red sector, May 31, 1892.
Keeper Chester Rowland falls into the water after returning to the station on August 3, 1908; body found three days later at Whitehead Point (LighthouseFriends).
November 2, 1914: keeper Louis P. Brown towed a disabled launch to safety in a northwest gale.
February 1918: a cake of ice strikes the station; $12,800 damage found the following spring (LighthouseFriends).
Light automated; maintenance given to Coast Guard personnel at Eaton's Neck.
Wooden tower removed from the caisson in 1965.
Steel skeleton tower erected on the caisson.
Wooden tower sold for $1 to a Centre Island resident (not named here) and moved ashore.
USLHS record only: skeletal structure on the old foundation in 1926. LighthouseFriends and Bachand date the steel replacement to 1965; not adopted.

corrections.current: tower, caisson, wood, built 1890, 11.0 m, standing
corrections.proposed: wooden tower moved ashore to private land on Centre Island in 1965; caisson and steel skeleton tower at the original site
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends and Bachand say the wooden tower was moved off the caisson in 1965 and is on private land on Centre Island, so it does not stand at the site. What remains at the original site is the caisson and a metal superstructure.
USLHS gives 41 feet above water at mean high water (12.5 m); LighthouseFriends gives forty-and-a-half feet (12.3 m). The record's 11.3 m matches neither.

corrections.proposed: F W with fixed red sector (from 31 May 1892)
corrections.why: The Light-House Board's 1892 report records the change from fixed red to fixed white with a fixed red sector.

resolved_conflicts.field: conflicts: 'A source says this structure is gone, but OpenStreetMap maps it today.'
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The wooden tower is gone from the site: it was moved ashore to Centre Island in 1965. The map point is the caisson, and what stands there is a steel skeleton tower (LighthouseFriends; Bachand).

notes_for_editor: 1) Conflicts. (a) USLHS place record 'Disposition' says the skeletal structure replaced the light 'in 1926 on Old Foundation'; LighthouseFriends and Bachand say 1965. The story uses 1965 and states the USLHS 1926 date. (b) Chester Rowland: the roster ends his stint July 31, 1908; LighthouseFriends has him returning August 3, 1908 and found three days later. (c) Ice night: Bachand says February 19, 1918; LighthouseFriends says February 25 (the story states both). Brown's Bulletin letter (1918, p. 26) refers to a February gale and the light out from 1:45 to 2:55 a.m. (OCR garbles the day; the lantern-out time is read as 26 February). (d) Louis P. Brown (roster and Bulletins) vs Louis R. Brown (Bachand; probably OCR). (e) Focal height: record 11.3 m vs USLHS 41 ft (12.5 m) and LighthouseFriends forty-and-a-half feet. The 1888 vs 1889 date for the offshore decision (Bachand vs LighthouseFriends) is stated in the story. The 1914 rescue is in the December 1914 Bulletin (No. 36), not November. The tower's removal accounts differ (LighthouseFriends: barge stuck on a sandbar for almost a year; Bachand: found floating and dragged across a marsh by truck winch) and the story states both. Range: record gives 8.0 nm; no source read gives a range. (f) Wooden tower height: record 11.0 m vs USLHS 38 ft (11.6 m); not corrected. (g) Status: USLHS says 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No'; no source read says whether the steel tower is lit. Coast Guard light list not read. 2) Bachand's 1934 account of a complaint about Keeper E.J. Smith and a stopped fog signal is in the article but is too scrambled in the OCR to quote, so it is not in the story. Check the original before use. 3) The 1965 buyer is named by LighthouseFriends and Bachand; the story does not name a private resident of a converted lighthouse (guide rule). 4) The Roosevelt visits rest only on LighthouseFriends; no primary source read. 5) The 1875 appropriation is not in the corpus (the Light-House Board volumes begin in 1891) and rests on LighthouseFriends; the Coast Guard Historian's chronology, which the search index shows (archived copy not readable), gives March 3, 1875. 6) Chronicling America was not searched for the 1908 drowning or the 1890 lighting. 7) The Life-Saving Service tables list 'Cold Spring Harbor' under Long Island Sound strandings; a 1908 line names Cold Spring Harbor, New Jersey, and the 1896 line names a Sabine Pass bar; neither is this station and neither is used. 8) The Lighthouse Board's 1891 entry for a bell buoy at Cold Spring Harbor (December 12, 1891) is an aid nearby, not the light; not used. 9) Wikipedia is a lead only and is not cited.
